package_info.package_manager: source (upstream C library, used by many Linux distributions)
package_info.why_malicious: The package was compromised by a rogue contributor who introduced an obfuscated backdoor into the upstream source code. This backdoor enabled unauthorized remote access to systems using the affected library, including critical infrastructure such as OpenSSH Server. The malicious code was intentionally hidden and designed to evade detection, representing a direct compromise of the software supply chain.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the library is loaded and used by dependent software, e.g., OpenSSH Server)
execution_context.file_location: obfuscated code within the liblzma source files (e.g., configure.ac, test files, or C source files)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Obfuscated C code that, when triggered, modifies the behavior of the library to allow for remote code execution or unauthorized access. (Exact code not shown in the report, but public analysis indicates the use of complex preprocessor macros and hidden payloads in test files and build scripts.)
malicious_snippets.code_language: C (with shell script elements in build system)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code hooks into the library's normal operation, intercepts authentication or command execution flows, and enables a remote attacker to bypass authentication or execute arbitrary code, resulting in a backdoor in systems using the compromised library.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is intentionally obfuscated and hidden within non-obvious parts of the codebase, such as test files and build scripts, and alters core authentication or execution logic in a way that is not documented or expected.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal library code should not contain obfuscated logic that alters authentication or execution flows, nor should it introduce undocumented remote access capabilities.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in rare cases for anti-tampering or DRM, but never in open source compression libraries or authentication modules.
key_indicators: Obfuscated code in core library files
Modification of authentication or execution logic
No legitimate documentation or rationale for changes

attack_chain.action: Rogue contributor gains trust and submits code changes to the upstream repository.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is merged into the main codebase.

attack_chain.action: Obfuscated malicious code is added to the library source and build scripts.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is included in official releases.

attack_chain.action: Downstream projects (e.g., OpenSSH Server) build and distribute software using the compromised library.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is deployed to end-user systems.

attack_chain.action: At runtime, the malicious code enables unauthorized remote access or code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains backdoor access to affected systems (final goal).

Unexpected changes in test or build scripts

network_indicators: Indirect: Unusual authentication bypass or remote code execution via services using the library (e.g., OpenSSH Server)
No direct network communication from the library itself, but enables network-based attacks
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for obfuscated or undocumented code changes in core library files, especially in upstream forks or new releases. Use static analysis to flag non-standard macros, hidden payloads, or code that alters authentication/execution logic. Review build and test scripts for unexpected additions. Monitor downstream software (e.g., OpenSSH) for abnormal authentication behavior or signs of unauthorized access after library updates.
